messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Juan, a 40-year-old Latin American surgeon married to his high school sweetheart, has been struggling with symptoms following a devastating natural disaster that shook his community last year. The event was traumatic for many, but for Juan, the aftermath has taken an especially heavy toll on both his personal life and his career. The night of the disaster was unforgettable: a powerful earthquake that triggered a series of fires across the city. Juan remembers the intense rumbling, followed by the piercing sound of sirens and the acrid smell of smoke filling the air. The memory is seared into his mind, but it’s only part of what he feels when he encounters certain triggers in his daily life. Loud noises, such as construction work or even sudden door slams at home, can instantly plunge Juan back into the chaos of that night. These moments are often followed by an overwhelming grief that washes over him, a stark reminder of lives lost and things left unspoken. The smell of smoke or burnt wood is equally potent; it brings back fragments of the disaster with such clarity that he feels like only parts of what happened are within his grasp, leaving much else as a painful void. Juan has come to rely on various coping mechanisms to manage these intrusive memories and the intense emotions they evoke. One night after a particularly loud thunderstorm, Juan turned to alcohol to numb the grief and anxiety, finding temporary solace in its embrace. Over time, he began to use sexual fantasies or engage in activities that offered an escape from his distressing thoughts. Distraction has also become a go-to strategy; he often turns on loud music or engrosses himself in puzzles or video games to keep the memories at bay. However, these strategies have not been without consequences. While they offer temporary relief, they do little to address the underlying issues and can sometimes exacerbate his symptoms. After a few drinks or hours of distraction, Juan finds that the grief lingers and can feel even more intense once he sobers up or turns off the television. In his professional life as a surgeon, these triggers have become particularly problematic. The smell of antiseptic in the operating room often evokes the acrid smoke from the fires, making it difficult for him to focus on surgery. He’s found himself cancelling procedures and taking time away from work, leading to strained relationships with colleagues who are increasingly concerned about his well-being. What frightens Juan most is the unpredictability of these triggers and the way they can overwhelm him without warning. The memory fragments and intense grief that follow feel like a relentless cycle he cannot break free from. He has started to wonder if he will ever be able to return to the operating table or even handle routine tasks at home. Despite his efforts to cope, Juan’s symptoms have grown increasingly unbearable. His wife has noticed changes in him and urged him to seek help, concerned about his emotional well-being and how it affects their family life. What brings Juan into therapy is a deep-seated fear of losing himself completely, but also a glimmer of hope that with the right support, he can regain control over his life and find peace. Juan’s journey towards healing begins with understanding these triggers and the cycle they have created in his life. He hopes to learn new ways to manage his distressing memories and avoid relying on maladaptive strategies that ultimately do more harm than good.
